XPENG’s humanoid robot, known as IRON, represents the company’s expansion beyond electric vehicles into robotics and embodied AI. XPENG, a Chinese EV manufacturer founded in 2014, has leveraged its expertise in electric drivetrains, AI software, and autonomous systems to develop robotic platforms capable of dynamic movement and real-time environmental interaction. Humanoid robots like IRON rely on advanced motion planning algorithms, electric actuators, and sensor fusion systems - typically combining cameras, LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and force sensors. These systems allow the robot to maintain balance, adjust posture, and perform coordinated movements that appear fluid and human-like. Modern humanoid locomotion depends heavily on real-time feedback control. Small positional corrections are made hundreds of times per second to stabilize joints and prevent falls. This is similar to the control architecture used in self-balancing robots and autonomous vehicles. XPENG’s broader robotics initiative aligns with a global push toward general-purpose humanoid platforms - machines designed to operate in human environments rather than factory-only settings. While still in early development stages, such robots are being researched for applications ranging from logistics and manufacturing to service roles and human-robot interaction studies. Replying to @fantic_hugoww Worked for 3m 18s techniahqrobot on x  This small humanoid robot is being pushed far beyond a normal walking demo. The test begins with direct impacts and repeated disturbances. A person swings a wooden stick toward the robot while the machine tries to stay upright, protect its posture and recover its balance. When it falls, the key is how the control system handles the loss of stability, how quickly the joints react and whether the robot can reduce damage during contact with the ground. Humanoid robots are difficult to control because every movement affects the whole body. A sudden hit on the shoulder changes the position of the torso, hips, knees and feet at the same time. The robot must estimate its orientation, detect joint position, calculate a response and send torque commands to several motors within milliseconds. A slow reaction can turn a small disturbance into a complete collapse. This type of test matters because clean laboratory walking is only one part of real-world robotics. A machine working in a factory, warehouse, school or public space may face slippery floors, uneven surfaces, accidental contact, moving objects and unexpected human behavior. Engineers need to know what happens when the robot is disturbed, not only when every condition is perfect. The video also shows an important limit. Surviving an impact does not prove that a humanoid robot understands the situation. It does not automatically demonstrate general intelligence, independent decision-making or safe operation around people. What we can observe is physical robustness, balance control and recovery behavior under a controlled disturbance. Those are valuable capabilities, but they are only part of a complete robotic system. Durability involves more than a strong outer shell. The motors, gearboxes, bearings, cables, batteries, sensors and onboard computer must continue working after vibration and impact. The software also needs safe fall behavior, joint limits, emergency stopping and reliable recovery routines. A robot that stands up quickly but swings its limbs unpredictably could still create a safety risk. Serious testing should measure both performance and safety. How much force can the structure absorb? Can the robot detect that a person is close? Does it reduce motor power before falling? Can an operator stop it instantly? Are the results repeated across many trials? One dramatic demonstration can look impressive, but repeatability is what turns a prototype into dependable hardware. Compact humanoids are useful research platforms because developers can study locomotion, reinforcement learning, robot perception, motion planning and human-robot interaction without using a full-size machine. Smaller platforms can still reveal major problems in dynamic balance, sim-to-real transfer, actuator control and recovery after disturbances. The next step should be controlled behavior: remain balanced when possible, fall safely when necessary, avoid people, protect critical components and recover only when the area is clear. Would you trust a humanoid robot more after seeing this durability test, or does this aggressive testing make you more concerned about how powerful these machines could become? I spent days teaching a 3D-printed robot duck to walk. Most of that time, it was falling over. It’s my own build of the Open Duck Mini. The open-source, BDX-inspired biped created by Antoine Pirrone. The whole thing is 3D-printed and runs on hobby-grade servos instead of industrial actuators, which is what makes it buildable on a normal budget and also what makes it so hard to get walking. The hard part wasn’t the printing or the assembly. It was the sim-to-real gap. A gait that walks perfectly in MuJoCo hits real-world joint slop, servo lag, and a center of mass that won’t sit still, and just before you know it, the duck face plants into the floor. It took me 40+ calibration passes before it could take three steps without tipping! What the build came down to: • 3D-printed chassis • Per-joint offset calibration (where most of the pain lived) • Policy training in simulation (MuJoCo / Isaac Lab) • Build guide + docs via Tnkr • A lot of failed walks Real hardware. Real failures. Real progress.

A humanoid robot named Joko Prabuwesi went viral after a video showed it unleashing a series of fast Shaolin-style martial arts kicks at office workers inside a corporate headquarters over the weekend. The robot lunged at staff as they struggled to hold it back while it carried out the choreographed combat moves. At first, many people thought the footage was AI-generated or a digital animation because of how realistic it looked. Later, independent technical verification confirmed the video was real and showed an actual robot moving inside a real workplace. Although the robot's smooth movements, balance and joint control were genuine, it wasn't acting on its own or experiencing a malfunction. Handlers from an Indonesian digital media company said the scene was a pre-programmed marketing demonstration to show off the robot's motor control. The kung fu routine had been loaded into its memory before the event.
